strengths: The paper tackles an interesting and underexplored problem: animating internal muscle anatomy from external visual/surface observations. The framing is timely for digital humans, biomechanics-aware capture, and graphics/vision applications where surface-only body models are insufficient.

The proposed SKIM capture pipeline is a meaningful contribution. The combination of multi-view RGB, an ArUco-embedded suit, dense temporally tracked surface correspondences, subject-specific scans, pose estimates, marker visibility, and anatomical bindings could be valuable to the community if released as promised.

The SOMA formulation is technically coherent: it separates muscle and skin deformation fields, supervises canonical residuals from tracked markers, and uses smoothness, tangential, stretching, bending, and volume-inspired regularizers to address the severe ambiguity of inferring internal deformation from surface observations.

The paper is generally clear and well organized, with helpful figures explaining the dataset, anatomical layers, model pipeline, and qualitative outputs. The limitations section is candid about dependence on initialization, the marker suit, and subject-specific training.

The results demonstrate plausible dynamic behavior and improved median/extreme marker tracking and volume/intersection metrics compared with the chosen baselines, suggesting the system is promising as a first step toward data-driven anatomical performance capture.
weaknesses: The central claim of recovering muscle deformation from visual data is only indirectly validated. There is no dynamic internal ground truth from MRI/ultrasound/other imaging, so the reported evidence mainly shows that the model fits sparse surface markers while satisfying hand-designed anatomical priors. This leaves uncertainty about whether the inferred muscle motions are anatomically correct rather than merely plausible.

The evaluation is limited in scale and generality: the dataset has only five subjects and the method is explicitly person-specific. The paper does not convincingly demonstrate cross-subject generalization, robustness to body shape variation, clothing/suit placement variation, or markerless/in-the-wild inputs, despite motivating scalable RGB-based digital humans.

The baseline comparison is not fully satisfying. HIT is a static/generic internal tissue estimator and appears disadvantaged by topology/template mismatch, while LBS is a very simple lower bound. The paper would be stronger with comparisons to more carefully adapted subject-specific anatomy transfer, simulation-driven deformation, or learned pose-corrective baselines under matched inputs.

Some quantitative results weaken the case: LBS has slightly better mean global marker error than SOMA, and the architecture ablation shows Linear, MLP, and U-Net variants are very close on marker accuracy. This suggests much of the observed benefit may come from the capture data and regularizers rather than the proposed neural architecture.

Several plausibility metrics are closely tied to the optimization objectives, especially volume preservation and intersection penalties. Improvements on these metrics are useful but not fully independent evidence of anatomical validity. More external validation, biomechanical expert assessment, held-out motions with stronger statistical reporting, or physical simulation comparison would make the scientific case stronger.

Important implementation and reproducibility details seem deferred to the supplementary material, including marker post-processing, binding of individual muscles, metric definitions, baseline configurations, and hyperparameters. Given the complexity of the pipeline, the main paper would benefit from more detail on sensitivity to template fitting errors, marker visibility, number of cameras, and loss weights.

strengths: The paper tackles an interesting and underexplored computer vision/graphics problem: linking observable surface deformation to dynamic internal muscle geometry. The overall direction is potentially valuable for digital humans, sports/medical visualization, and animation.

The SKIM capture setup is a notable practical contribution. Dense ArUco suit tracking, multi-view capture, subject-specific scans, skeletal poses, marker trajectories, visibility masks, and anatomical bindings could be useful if released with enough documentation.

The method is reasonably coherent as a subject-specific deformation model: it combines pose-conditioned corrective blendshapes with smoothness, tangential, stretch, bending, and volume-inspired priors, and the decomposition into skin and muscle layers is a plausible engineering design.

The paper includes ablations over architecture and regularization terms, and it is transparent about several important limitations, including dependence on fitted anatomy, the marker suit, and subject-specific training.
weaknesses: The central claim of recovering internal muscle deformation from visual observations is not convincingly validated. There is no dynamic internal ground truth from MRI/ultrasound/other measurement, so the evaluation mostly demonstrates marker fitting plus satisfaction of the authors' own geometric priors, not anatomical correctness of the predicted muscles.

The practical setup substantially weakens the framing as RGB-based or scalable vision. The pipeline relies on a custom marker suit, a 120-camera studio, a separate 140-camera scanner, subject-specific anatomical fitting, and ground-truth skeletal pose. This is far from ordinary RGB input, and the paper sometimes overstates accessibility and generality.

The dataset scale and generalization evidence are limited. SKIM contains only five subjects, and the reported generalization appears to be to unseen motions for trained subject-specific models, not to unseen people or markerless/in-the-wild settings. This is a serious limitation for a parametric human model claim.

The quantitative results are not as strong as the narrative suggests. In Table 2, LBS has slightly better mean global tracking error than SOMA, intersection ratios are essentially identical for LBS and SOMA, and SOMA has much worse muscle-to-bone volume deviation than HIT. The paper emphasizes favorable columns but does not sufficiently discuss these mixed results.

The baseline comparison is weak. HIT is a static/body-surface implicit tissue estimator and appears mismatched to the task; the paper uses cross-topology interpolation and reports extremely poor tracking for HIT, making the comparison hard to interpret. Stronger baselines such as pose-space deformation variants, learned surface residual models, per-subject neural deformation without anatomy priors, or simulation-trained models would be needed.

The anatomical template itself comes from volumetric fitting rather than measured subject-specific internal anatomy. Since individual muscles are then deformed by propagating from a global boundary layer, the method may produce plausible-looking anatomy without demonstrating correct muscle origins, insertions, volumes, or activations.

Several metrics are potentially circular. Volume preservation, interpenetration, and smoothness-like behavior are also training priors, so good performance on these measures does not independently establish biological realism.

Important reproducibility details seem deferred to supplementary material: marker counts and coverage, train/test splits, network architecture specifics, loss weights, optimization details, filtering parameters, baseline configuration, and dataset release terms. For a method with many coupled components, the main paper leaves too much unspecified.

The writing is generally understandable but occasionally overclaims, for example using language such as 'guarantees internal physical plausibility' and 'recover muscle deformations' despite lacking direct internal validation. There is also some repetition and minor polish issues in the method section.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and underexplored problem: inferring dynamic internal muscle deformation from accessible surface observations. The proposed combination of SKIM and SOMA is novel and relevant to computer vision, graphics, biomechanics-aware human modeling, and digital humans.

The SKIM capture pipeline is a strong contribution. Dense ArUco suit tracking, subject-specific skin/bone/muscle meshes, skeletal poses, marker trajectories, residual fields, and visibility masks provide a rare bridge between external surface motion and internal anatomical structure.

The SOMA formulation is technically thoughtful: decoupled muscle and skin deformation layers, canonical residual supervision, and biomechanically inspired regularizers for smoothness, tangential behavior, stretching, intersections, and volume preservation are well motivated.

The experimental evidence supports the main claim that the method improves dynamic soft-tissue behavior over simple LBS and a generic internal-tissue baseline. The ablations are useful and show that the physical priors materially improve volume preservation and stability.

The work is clearly written overall, with good figures, a coherent problem setup, and an honest limitations section acknowledging dependence on template fitting, marker suits, and subject-specific training.
weaknesses: The evaluation is constrained by the absence of true dynamic volumetric muscle ground truth. This is understandable, but it means the strongest anatomical claims are supported mainly by surface marker tracking and plausibility metrics rather than direct validation of internal muscle deformation.

The dataset is small, with five subjects and subject-specific models. This limits evidence for generalization across body shapes, soft-tissue distributions, motions, and clothing/contact conditions, and weakens claims about scalability beyond controlled capture.

The method is described as recovering muscle deformation from RGB observations, but the actual supervision relies on a custom marker-embedded suit, multi-camera studio capture, ground-truth skeletal poses, and subject-specific anatomical fitting. The paper could more sharply distinguish this controlled surface-tracking setting from ordinary markerless RGB video.

Baselines are somewhat limited. LBS is a low-end kinematic baseline, while HIT is not designed for dynamic subject-specific muscle motion; stronger comparisons to simulation-based or learned pose-corrective soft-tissue models, where feasible, would better contextualize the gains.

Some implementation details appear relegated to supplementary material, including marker post-processing, baseline configuration, and binding/deformation of individual muscles. These details are important for reproducibility and for assessing whether the reported results depend on sensitive engineering choices.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and underexplored problem: going beyond surface-only human body models to infer dynamic internal muscle deformation from accessible visual observations. This is original and potentially impactful for digital humans, biomechanics-aware animation, sports/medical visualization, and performance capture.

The proposed SKIM capture setup is a meaningful systems contribution. The custom ArUco suit, multi-view capture, subject-specific scanned templates, marker trajectories, visibility masks, skeletal poses, and muscle correspondence annotations form a useful dataset direction, especially because dynamic full-body soft-tissue data is scarce.

The SOMA formulation is technically coherent at a high level: canonical residual supervision, decoupled skin/muscle layers, pose-conditioned deformation networks, and geometric/volume regularizers are reasonable design choices for this ill-posed inverse problem.

The paper includes relevant ablations over architecture and regularization terms, and the limitations section honestly acknowledges important issues such as dependence on marker suits, subject-specific training, template initialization, and missing force/co-contraction modeling.

Qualitative figures and the interactive visualization tool suggest that the method can produce plausible muscle/skin deformation effects in real time, which supports the applied/systems value of the work.
weaknesses: The central claim of recovering muscle deformation from RGB/video is not directly validated. The supervision comes from external suit markers and the internal anatomy is generated from template fitting, while no dynamic in-vivo muscle ground truth, medical validation, EMG/activation evidence, or biomechanical simulation reference is used to establish that the inferred muscle deformations are anatomically correct.

The muscle/skin decomposition remains underconstrained. Only surface marker residuals supervise the model, while the internal muscle layer is shaped primarily by priors. The paper acknowledges ambiguity but does not convincingly show that the learned decomposition corresponds to true muscle behavior rather than one plausible regularized explanation of surface motion.

The experimental comparison is limited. The main baselines are LBS and HIT, but HIT is a static/internal tissue estimator and appears poorly matched to the subject-specific high-resolution setup. There is no comparison to data-driven surface deformation models, physics-based simulation approximations, learned pose-corrective blendshapes without internal layers, or stronger marker-driven reconstruction baselines.

The quantitative results are mixed and sometimes do not fully support the narrative. LBS has slightly lower MPME than SOMA, intersection ratios for LBS and SOMA are nearly identical, and the volume/intersection metrics are largely consequences of the proposed regularizers rather than independent evidence of anatomical accuracy.

Generalization evidence is weak. The evaluation appears to be on unseen sequences for the same subject-specific models, not unseen subjects or markerless RGB inputs. Since the method is person-specific and trained with a marker suit, the practical gap to the claimed scalable RGB-based setting remains substantial.

The dataset is small in subject diversity: five subjects with limited demographics. This is understandable for a complex capture system, but it constrains claims about full-body anatomical generality and person-agnostic applicability.

The individual-muscle animation step is only a barycentric propagation from the global muscle boundary to high-resolution muscle meshes. This may be useful visually, but the paper does not validate whether specific muscles deform correctly, whether origins/insertions are preserved, or whether antagonistic/synergistic muscles behave physiologically.

Some methodological details that affect reproducibility and interpretation are underspecified or deferred: train/validation split protocol, per-subject training details, exact marker coverage effects on different body regions, sensitivity to template fitting errors, and whether code/data release includes all assets needed to reproduce the pipeline.

strengths: The paper addresses an interesting and underexplored problem: connecting observable surface motion to internal anatomical deformation for digital humans. The idea of collecting dense, temporally consistent surface correspondences with an ArUco suit is practically useful, and the SKIM capture setup could be valuable if released with sufficient documentation.

The proposed representation combines skin, global muscle, bone layers, and individual muscle meshes in a coherent animation pipeline. The loss terms for smoothness, stretch, tangential motion, and volume preservation are reasonable graphics/biomechanics-inspired priors, and the qualitative visualizations suggest the system can produce plausible subject-specific animations.

The manuscript is generally understandable and includes ablations over architecture and regularization terms, plus a limitations section acknowledging the marker suit, subject-specific training, and lack of force/co-contraction modeling.
weaknesses: The central claim of recovering muscle deformation from RGB/surface observations is not convincingly supported. There is no dynamic ground-truth muscle deformation from MRI, ultrasound, implanted markers, validated FEM, EMG, or other physiological measurement. The model is supervised only by sparse surface marker residuals and regularized by hand-designed priors, so the inferred internal muscle motion is largely unvalidated and may be visually plausible rather than anatomically correct.

The formulation is fundamentally pose-driven at inference, so it cannot resolve many-to-one biomechanical ambiguity: different activations, loads, fatigue states, or co-contractions can produce different muscle shapes at the same skeletal pose. This directly undercuts the stated goal of recovering muscle behavior from surface observations, especially since the dataset includes weighted exercises where load should matter but the model input appears to be only pose.

The quantitative results are weak and sometimes contradict the claims. SOMA has worse global MPME than LBS (13.43 vs. 13.11), worse DRE at the >15mm threshold than HIT, the same intersection ratio as LBS, and much worse deep muscle-to-bone volume change than HIT (10.35% vs. 1.95%). The paper nevertheless frames the method as clearly resolving tracking and plausibility issues, which is not borne out by the table.

The evaluation metrics are not sufficient evidence for internal anatomical correctness. Intersection and volume preservation mostly measure compliance with the model's own geometric priors, not biological validity. Marker tracking evaluates the skin layer, not muscles. Qualitative comparisons to HIT are difficult to interpret because of topology and template differences, and the baseline setup seems unfavorable to HIT/SMPL compared with subject-specific scanned templates.

The dataset is very small for the breadth of the claims: only five subjects, limited demographics, and subject-specific models. There is no convincing cross-subject or held-out-subject evaluation, yet the introduction emphasizes scalability and RGB-based recovery. The practical capture setup also requires a dense custom marker suit and a 120-camera studio, which is far from the accessible multi-view RGB scenario implied by the abstract.

The novelty over pose-space deformation/blendshapes plus anatomical template fitting is limited. The method is essentially a subject-specific pose-to-displacement network regularized with standard smoothness/stretch/volume terms. The paper does not clearly establish a technical advance commensurate with the strong claims about internal muscle recovery.

Important experimental details are underspecified or questionable: train/validation split protocol, per-subject performance, marker visibility effects on metrics, statistical variation, random seeds, and how missing markers affect supervision. The U-Net terminology is also unclear because the described input is a flattened pose vector rather than a spatial signal with obvious convolutional structure.

The manuscript has presentation and consistency issues: repeated sentences, awkward wording, duplicated references, future-dated or incomplete citations, inconsistent dataset counts, and overclaiming in relation to the evidence. These issues are not merely cosmetic because they make it harder to assess reproducibility and attribution.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and underexplored vision problem: inferring dynamic internal muscle/anatomical deformation from observable surface motion. This is a meaningful direction for digital humans, biomechanics-aware avatars, sports/medical visualization, and performance capture.

Although no contribution type is explicitly declared, I would assess this primarily as an Applied/Systems plus Dataset/Benchmark contribution rather than only an Algorithms/General paper. Under that lens, the custom SKIM capture setup, subject-specific anatomical templates, tracked marker residuals, and promised code/data release are substantial and increase the paper's value.

The proposed SOMA representation is technically sensible: decoupling muscle and skin deformation, supervising canonical residuals, and adding smoothness, tangential, stretch, biharmonic, and volume-preservation priors directly address the ill-posed nature of skin-to-muscle inference.

The dataset and supplementary material provide useful detail on subject demographics, capture protocol, marker encoding, mesh sizes, preprocessing, metrics, hyperparameters, and baseline setup, which supports reproducibility better than many systems papers.

The experimental results show convincing practical benefits over simple LBS and a static internal-tissue baseline, especially in median/P90 tracking error, dynamic regions, volume preservation, and qualitative muscle-specific visualization. The ablations support the importance of the physical regularizers.
weaknesses: The central claim of recovering muscle deformation from RGB/surface observations remains only indirectly validated. There is no dynamic volumetric ground truth, EMG/activation validation, ultrasound/MRI spot check, or biomechanical force comparison, so the inferred muscles are plausible but not conclusively anatomically correct.

The method is subject-specific and depends on a custom marker suit, high-end 120-camera capture, static body scanning, and volumetric template fitting. This limits scalability and weakens claims about accessible RGB-based recovery, even though the authors acknowledge this limitation.

The evaluation uses only five subjects and does not clearly report cross-subject generalization, train/test motion splits, variance across subjects, or robustness to reduced camera counts/marker visibility. This makes it hard to judge how stable the approach is beyond the captured setting.

The baselines are somewhat limited. LBS is a weak lower bound, and HIT via SMPL is disadvantaged by template/topology mismatch and being designed for static tissue estimation. Comparisons to stronger pose-corrective surface models, subject-specific learned deformation baselines, or simulation-based approximations would make the empirical case stronger.

Some quantitative claims are stronger than the table strictly supports: for example, global MPME is slightly worse than LBS, and the table formatting/column interpretation for DRE and volume metrics is not fully clear. The paper would benefit from clearer per-metric discussion and statistical reporting.

The internal individual-muscle deformation is propagated from a learned boundary layer via barycentric binding, which may not capture true muscle-specific contraction, sliding, or co-contraction effects. This is a reasonable engineering choice, but it should temper claims about individual muscle behavior.
